summary: This document extends OWAMP and TWAMP to measure performance on every member link of a Link Aggregation Group. Knowing each link's metrics lets operators steer traffic across member links based on performance.

plainLanguage.summary: When a road has several lanes, you test the speed of each lane to send cars to the fastest. This does so for bundled network links.

questions: what is a micro session in twamp
how to measure each lag member link
subtitle: Measuring delay, jitter and loss on every individual link of a bundled connection, not just the bundle as a whole.

tldr.problem: A Link Aggregation Group spreads traffic over several physical links, but a normal OWAMP or TWAMP test cannot tell how each member link performs. Without that, operators cannot steer time-sensitive traffic to the best link.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines micro sessions, one OWAMP or TWAMP session per member link, set up with two new control commands. Micro TWAMP test packets carry two new 2-octet member link identifiers so both ends can validate which link a packet used.
tldr.outcome: Operators get the usual delay, jitter and packet loss metrics for each member link of a LAG, which supports performance-based traffic steering across the links.

today: RFC 9533 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2024. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The same idea for STAMP is in RFC 9534.

sections.title: Why Measure Each Member Link
sections.content:
A Link Aggregation Group (LAG) combines several physical links into one logical link. It gives more bandwidth and better resiliency: if one member link fails, the others keep forwarding traffic. Traffic is usually spread over the members with a hash-based mechanism.

The delay can differ between member links because they may take different transport paths, especially in a wide area network. To give low-latency service to time-sensitive traffic, an operator needs to steer traffic across the member links based on delay, loss and similar metrics. That needs a measurement of every member link, which can then work together with the Layer 2 bundle member link attributes of RFC 8668.

OWAMP (RFC 4656) and TWAMP (RFC 5357) are active measurement methods. A single test session over a LAG can use a specially constructed 5-tuple to measure one member link, but without knowledge of each member link it cannot measure every physical link. This RFC extends both protocols to close that gap, and it provides the same metrics as they do, such as delay, jitter and packet loss.
sections.plainLanguage: A bundle of links is like a road with several lanes. Some lanes are faster than others, so we want to time each lane on its own.

sections.title: Micro Sessions on a LAG
sections.content:
The RFC covers the case where a LAG directly connects two nodes. To measure every member link, one session per member link is established between the two endpoints. These are called micro sessions. They are ordinary OWAMP or TWAMP sessions running on member links, with one addition: test packets of micro TWAMP sessions MUST carry member link information for validation.

All micro sessions of a LAG share the same Sender IP Address and Receiver IP Address. For UDP ports, they may share one Sender Port and Receiver Port pair, or each may have its own pair. The shared pair is simpler to operate and is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one test for the whole road, we run one small test in each lane. All the little tests start and end at the same two places.

sections.title: Micro OWAMP Sessions
sections.content:
Micro OWAMP adds a new control command, Request-OW-Micro-Sessions with value 5. It is based on the OWAMP Request-Session command and uses the same message format from Section 3.5 of RFC 4656. Session creation follows the same procedure with one addition: when an OWAMP Server accepts the request, it MUST build a set of micro sessions for all the member links of the LAG on which the request arrived.

For testing, micro OWAMP reuses the OWAMP-Test packet format and procedures. The Session-Sender MUST send test packets over the member link the session is associated with. The Session-Receiver MUST use the member link a packet arrived on to find the matching micro session, and if none exists the packet MUST be discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: One request tells the other end to start a test in every lane. A packet that shows up in a lane with no test running is simply thrown away.

sections.title: Micro TWAMP Packets
sections.content:
Micro TWAMP adds the control command Request-TW-Micro-Sessions with value 11, based on the TWAMP Request-Session command (Section 3.5 of RFC 5357). As with OWAMP, an accepting server MUST build micro sessions for all member links of the LAG that received the request.

The test packets add two new fields to the TWAMP Session-Sender and Session-Reflector formats, in both unauthenticated and authenticated modes: Sender Micro-session ID and Reflector Micro-session ID. Each is 2 octets long and carries the LAG member link identifier of that side. Each value MUST be unique within a TWAMP session at the Session-Sender or Session-Reflector respectively. The RFC notes they may later be used for cases beyond LAGs. All other fields are as defined in RFC 5357.
sections.plainLanguage: Each test packet gets two name tags: one for the sender's lane and one for the reflector's lane, so everyone can tell which lane it used.

sections.title: Sender and Reflector Behavior
sections.content:
The micro Session-Sender inherits TWAMP Session-Sender behavior and MUST send its packets over the member link of its session. It puts its own member link identifier in the Sender Micro-session ID. If it knows the Reflector's identifier, it MUST set the Reflector Micro-session ID; otherwise that field MUST be zero. The RFC does not say how to learn the Reflector identifier: it can be preconfigured or learned from the data plane, such as from a reflected packet.

The micro Session-Reflector matches an incoming packet to a micro session using the member link it arrived on, and discards the packet if there is none. If the Reflector Micro-session ID is not zero, the Reflector validates it against that link, and discards the packet on failure. A zero value is not verified. When replying, it copies the Sender member link identifier into the Sender Micro-session ID and fills in its own identifier in the Reflector Micro-session ID.

When a reflected packet returns, the Sender uses the receiving member link to find the session, and discards the packet if there is none. It then validates the Sender Micro-session ID against the expected member link and the Reflector Micro-session ID to check the Reflector's behavior, discarding the packet if either check fails.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender and reflector each write their lane name on the packet and check the other side's tag. If a tag is wrong, the packet is thrown out.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA has allocated one new command number in each of two registries. In the OWAMP-Control Command Numbers registry, value 5 is Request-OW-Micro-Sessions. In the TWAMP-Control Command Numbers registry, value 11 is Request-TW-Micro-Sessions. Both reference this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of command numbers now has two new entries, one for each of the two new requests.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it does not introduce additional security requirements and mechanisms beyond those described in RFC 4656 and RFC 5357. The existing OWAMP and TWAMP protections apply as they are.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new to worry about here. The safety rules of the older protocols still apply.

messages.label: Test packet
messages.note: Carries the Sender Micro-session ID, and the Reflector Micro-session ID if known (otherwise zero).

messages.label: Reflected packet
messages.note: Copies the Sender ID and adds its own Reflector ID. The Sender validates both.
